migrationNotes: Spine: a delivery drone between A (1, 2) and B (4, 6) on a town grid. First the flight along the grid lines, then the straight flight as the hypotenuse of a triangle built from the two coordinate gaps, then points on both sides of zero, then what sliding a segment does.

lesson.title: Distance on a grid

steps.headline: How far apart on the grid

lead.text: A point on a grid is described by two numbers in brackets. The first says how far across the point is, and the second says how far up. So (2, 1) is two steps across and one step up from the place where the counting starts.

To find how far apart two points are in one direction, subtract. Take (2, 1) and (8, 4). The across numbers are 2 and 8, so the points are 8 − 2 = 6 units apart sideways. The up numbers are 1 and 4, so they are 4 − 1 = 3 units apart vertically. Each of these is a coordinate difference.

afterFigure.text: A negative coordinate puts a point on the other side of zero, so the gap has to be counted across zero. From −2 to 3 is 2 steps to reach zero and 3 more, which makes 5 units. Subtraction gives the same: 3 − (−2) = 5.

lead.text: Back to the drone, flying along the grid lines from A to B.

steps.headline: The straight flight is a hypotenuse

lead.text: The drone doesn't have to follow the streets. The route along the grid and the straight line from A to B make a right triangle. One leg is the sideways gap and the other is the vertical gap, and the two meet at a right angle because one runs across and the other runs straight up. The straight flight is the hypotenuse.
That puts the last lesson's rule to work. Take the points (1, 1) and (9, 16). The gaps are 9 − 1 = 8 and 16 − 1 = 15, so the distance is √(8² + 15²) = √(64 + 225) = √289 = 17 units.
A distance on a grid starts with subtraction, which gives the two gaps. The rest is the rule you already have. Square each gap and add the squares. Then take the square root of the sum.
The drone could fly straight from A (1, 2) to B (4, 6) instead of following the grid.

steps.headline: Points on either side of zero

lead.text: Negative coordinates cause most of the slips with distances, so it is worth working one through. Take the points (−5, −4) and (4, 8). The sideways gap runs across zero: 5 units to reach it and 4 more, which is 4 − (−5) = 9. The vertical gap does the same, since 8 − (−4) = 12.

The legs are 9 and 12. Squaring gives 81 and 144, and these add to 225. The square root of 225 is 15, so the points are 15 units apart. Dropping the minus sign from −5 would make the gap 4 − 5 = −1, and the distance would come out badly wrong.

A quick check helps here. When two coordinates lie on opposite sides of zero, the gap between them is their sizes added together, so it is larger than both. A smaller gap usually means a minus sign has been dropped.
Find how far apart the points are in each direction first, then use the right triangle they make.

Two more facts help with checking. The first is about moving a segment. Suppose the points (1, 1) and (4, 5) are both moved 5 units right and 3 units up, to (6, 4) and (9, 8). Each across number grew by 5, so their difference is still 9 − 6 = 3. Each up number grew by 3, so their difference is still 8 − 4 = 4. The gaps are 3 and 4 before and after, and so the distance is unchanged.

The second fact is about order. If you call the points the other way round, each subtraction comes out with the opposite sign. A square is never negative, so squaring the gaps wipes out the sign and the distance comes out the same. It doesn't matter which point you start from.
Both ends of a segment are moved: 2 units right and 1 unit up. Ask what happens to the gaps between them.

lesson.orientation: Use coordinate differences as right-triangle legs and distinguish direct distance from a grid path.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A delivery drone works in a town laid out like graph paper. Its base is marked A and the customer's house is marked B. Every place on the grid has two numbers, called its coordinates, which say how far across the point is and how far up. A is at (1, 2) and B is at (4, 6). On its usual route the drone keeps to the grid lines, flying east first and then north.

The drone's controller has no map to look at. It has two numbers for each place and has to work everything else out from them. It needs the distance along the grid lines, and it also needs the straight-line distance between A and B, which is the shortest flight it could make.

The last lesson gave a rule for the long side of a right triangle. This lesson shows that the rule works on a grid, where any two points are the corners of a right triangle that you can read straight from their coordinates.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how far apart two points are in a straight line, from their coordinates.

recap.keyIdea: Subtract coordinates to get the horizontal and vertical gaps, then use them as the legs of a right triangle.

blocks.text: The drone's route along the grid from A to B is 7 units, and the straight flight is 5.
You also found 17 units from (1, 1) to (9, 16), 25 from (0, 1) to (7, 25), and found that sliding both ends of a segment leaves its length alone.

recap.nextHook: Flat shapes have areas, and the next lesson moves on to boxes. It starts with sugar cubes stacked in layers and asks how many of them fill the box.

questions.prompt: A is at (1, 2) and B is at (4, 6). How many units apart are they horizontally?
hints: Horizontal position is the first coordinate.
Subtract the two x coordinates.
Find the absolute value of 4 − 1.
questions.onCorrect: 3. The horizontal gap is the difference of the x coordinates: 4 − 1.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is the sum of the x coordinates. Subtract them to find the gap.
4 is B's x coordinate. The distance is the gap between the two.

questions.prompt: How many units apart are A (1, 2) and B (4, 6) vertically?
hints: Vertical position is the second coordinate.
Subtract the two y coordinates.
Find the absolute value of 6 − 2.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The vertical gap is the difference of the y coordinates: 6 − 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the y coordinates. Subtract to find the gap.
6 is B's y coordinate. The distance is the gap between the two.

questions.prompt: Find the straight-line distance from A(1, 2) to B(4, 6), in grid units.
hints: Use the horizontal and vertical differences as legs.
Add the squares of the differences.
Calculate √((4 − 1)² + (6 − 2)²).
questions.onCorrect: 5 units. The differences 3 and 4 are legs, so the distance is the square root of 9 + 16.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 is the bent path, 3 across and 4 up. The straight line is shorter.
25 is the square of the distance. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: Both endpoints of a segment move 2 units right and 1 unit up. What happens to its length?
hints: What happens to the gap between the two ends?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same translation leaves both coordinate differences unchanged, so the length is unchanged.

questions.onCorrect: The length stays the same. Both ends move together, so the gaps between them do not change.

misconceptions.feedback: Moving both ends the same way doesn't stretch the segment. The gap between them stays the same.
Nothing is stretched. Both ends move together.

questions.prompt: Find the straight-line distance from (−3, 1) to (5, 7), in grid units.
hints: Subtract corresponding coordinates.
The x difference crosses from negative to positive.
questions.onCorrect: 10 units. Differences 8 and 6, then the square root of 64 + 36.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bent path, 8 across and 6 up. The straight line is shorter.
100 is the square of the distance. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: Find the straight-line distance from (−3, −4) to (2, 8), in grid units.
hints: Use coordinate differences, not their sum.
Square the horizontal and vertical separations.
questions.onCorrect: 13 units. Differences 5 and 12, then the square root of 25 + 144.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bent path, across then up. The straight line is shorter.
169 is the square of the distance. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: A drone flies from A (1, 2) to B (4, 6), going east first and then north. How many grid units does it fly?
hints: How far east does it go?
How far north does it go?
Add the two parts of the journey.
questions.onCorrect: 7. The drone flies 3 units east and 4 units north, and the two parts add.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds all four coordinates. Only the distance flown counts, not the positions.
That is the straight line between the two points, which the drone doesn't fly.

questions.prompt: Why are the two differences the legs of a right triangle?
hints: What angle do a horizontal and a vertical line make?

acceptedIdeas: Going across then up makes a right angle, and the direct line closes the triangle.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Going across then up makes a right angle, and the direct line closes the triangle.

choices.label: Going across then up makes a right angle, and the direct line closes the triangle.
Because the differences are always equal.
Because the direct line is horizontal.

questions.onCorrect: Across then up meet at a right angle. The straight line between the points is the hypotenuse.

misconceptions.feedback: They can be any two numbers. The right angle comes from going across and then up.
The direct line is slanted. It is the hypotenuse of the triangle.

questions.prompt: Find the straight-line distance from (0, 1) to (7, 25), in grid units.
hints: Find the horizontal and vertical differences.
Square both and add them.
Take the square root of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: 25 units. The differences are 7 and 24, and 49 + 576 = 625.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bent path, across then up. The straight line is shorter.
625 is the square of the distance. Take the square root.

questions.prompt: Two points are 12 units apart horizontally and 16 units apart vertically. How far apart are they in a straight line?
hints: The two separations are the legs of a right triangle.
Square both and add.
Take the square root of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: 20 units. The legs are 12 and 16, and 144 + 256 = 400.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bent path, across then up. The straight line is shorter.
400 is the square of the distance. Take the square root.
